summary: Fr. Dan Reehil, exorcist of the Diocese of Nashville, tells Fox News Digital that Ouija boards and other attempts to contact the dead are spiritually dangerous, not innocent games, because demons impersonate the dead and can enter a person's life. The article explains the Catholic Church's major and minor exorcisms and three levels of demonic incursion, and recounts the Ouija board's history from its 1890 naming and 1891 patent to its current production by Hasbro. Reehil says he has seen six cases of demonic oppression tied to Ouija use.
one_line: Nashville diocese exorcist Fr. Dan Reehil warns Ouija boards are a form of divination that invites demons, and the article traces the board's history.
key_facts: Fr. Dan Reehil is a priest of the Diocese of Nashville; in 2018 he received exorcism training at Ateneo Pontificio Regina Apostolorum in Rome and was installed as the diocese's exorcist that year.

Reehil says an exorcist is a priest chosen and installed by a bishop to exercise the office of deliverance ministry, and exorcism is a form of prayer the Catholic Church uses against the power of the devil.

The Catholic Church distinguishes major exorcisms, performed only for someone demonstrably possessed and only by a priest the bishop has permitted, from minor exorcisms, which are associated with sacraments and blessings.
Demonologists distinguish three levels of demonic incursion: temptation, obsession (also called oppression) and possession.
Reehil says 'Using an Ouija board is inviting a demon into your life, whether the person has that intention or not,' and that demons lie and impersonate dead people.
In 1890, Baltimore spiritualist and medium Helen Peters asked a talking board what to call it, and it answered 'O-U-I-J-A,' which it said meant 'good luck.'
The Ouija board patent was awarded on Feb. 10, 1891; legend says Peters and attorney Elijah Bond had the board spell out the patent officer's name, leaving him 'white-faced and visibly shaken.'
The Kennard Novelty Company mass-produced the boards and was sold to Parker Brothers in 1967; today Hasbro produces the Ouija board and markets it as a way to communicate with the 'spirit world.'
Fox News Digital reached out to Hasbro for comment but did not hear back by publication time.
Reehil says the Ouija board is 'far from' a typical game, calling it 'a form of divination,' and notes that the Bible condemns divination and occult practices numerous times.

The 1949 case of 'Roland Doe,' a teenage boy from Maryland who underwent numerous major exorcisms, is the most famous alleged Ouija-linked possession; it inspired William Peter Blatty's 1971 book 'The Exorcist' and the 1973 film starring Ellen Burstyn and Linda Blair.

Reehil says he has personally seen six cases of demonic oppression stemming from Ouija board use, with victims left with night terrors, suicidal ideation and despair, and one man impaled in the leg by chicken bones that flew across the kitchen.
Reehil says demonic activity ceased once deliverance prayers were prayed and participants renounced all participation with the demons.
